analysis.title: Eye on the Market: Califoreboding
key_insights: California has the third-highest state GDP growth over the last year at 3.6%, behind only New York and Idaho, largely attributable to AI, despite energy costs about 50% above the national median, the highest individual income tax rate, the highest state unemployment rate at 5.1% and the highest unsheltered homeless rate in the US.

A basket of 42 AI stocks accounts for 60%-80% of S&P 500 earnings growth, price returns and capital spending since January 2024. The chart shows 67% of price return, 58% of earnings growth and 81% of capex/R&D growth.

60% of S&P 500 stocks are down 20% or more from their all-time highs while the index is within 1% of its all-time high. Only 30% of stocks are outperforming the S&P 500 on a 3-year trailing basis, one of the lowest readings since 1991.

AI is primarily benefitting AI supply chain companies rather than the companies adopting it. The technology share of GDP growth has risen from almost zero to about 33% since 2022, and only 20% of US states are growing faster than the national average, almost the lowest since 1979.

AI-related construction (data centers and power) is the only positive construction category, up 38% since January 2024. Manufacturing is down 28%, commercial real estate down 13% and residential down 6%. The report flags the decline in planned data center projects as something to watch.

Net interest costs of US nonfinancial corporations are still at an all-time low share of corporate profits despite higher short-term rates. The report concludes the corporate sector seems more immune to rising short rates than in the past, at least so far.

Since January 2024, technology stocks globally have mostly been driven by earnings growth rather than P/E multiple expansion. The author says markets driven by earnings growth are less susceptible to rapid declines than those driven by multiples, though tech multiples are not cheap.
SpaceX is holding up better than most large tech IPOs at day 116 after its IPO, though only about 20% of its shares have been released into the free float, so it may be too early to judge.

Chinese auto brands are gaining market share in Europe. Per VW plant data, Tianjin labor cost is EUR 12/hour vs EUR 74 in Emden, and factory cost per vehicle is EUR 1,078 vs EUR 4,850. Tariffs of 17%-35% have done little to slow Chinese EV imports.

The EU is reportedly prepared to impose its own Section 301-style tariffs on China if China does not meet demands on voluntary export restrictions, rare earth licensing, overcapacity and market access. China may have the upper hand: it exports more rare earths and permanent magnets to Germany alone than to the US, and has opened anti-dumping investigations into European exports.

Anthropic reported that for under $5,000 its engineers 'abliterated' Z.AI's open-weight GLM 5.3, removing safety restrictions. Its harmful-request refusal rate fell to nearly 0% with no loss of reasoning performance. The author reads this as a pre-IPO push by Anthropic for regulation of competitor open-weight models, with no clear sign of Administration action.

The 10-year Treasury yield has broken through the level set by the August 19 Twist operation. The author attributes the rise to sticky inflation, hyperscaler debt issuance and above-expected GDP growth, and does not think the 'Final Act' for Federal debt is underway.

For the first time since 1970 the US budget deficit is worse than 5% of GDP and widening during an economic expansion. The CBO projects 100% of Federal tax revenues will be needed just for entitlements and interest by 2030-2031.

The author considers an eventual budget restructuring (tax increases and mandatory spending cuts, often means-tested) more likely than outright Fed debt monetization, and says it would be positive in the long run. Little discretionary spending is left to cut.

Private credit stress is measured differently by source. Providers such as KBRA, Lincoln International, S&P, Houlihan Lokey and Proskauer cite default rates of 1%-3%. Cliffwater's measure (non-accruals plus PIK loans marked at 96 or below) shows about 5%, and 70% of amended PIK loans never return to cash pay within two years.

JPMAM's own measure of BDC loan stress, built from five categories of stress, is about 15%, versus realized losses and write-offs of only 1%-2%. The author concludes that stress measures should include non-accruals, PIK conversions, maturity extensions and debt-to-equity conversions, and that investor returns will only be known after more price discovery.
The author doubts the 2026 US midterms will have substantial near-term impacts on financial markets regardless of the outcome.

sector_views.rationale: Earnings growth, not multiple expansion, has driven tech returns since January 2024, but AI concentration in market returns, earnings and capex is extreme and tech multiples are not cheap.
Chinese brands are taking share in Europe on a large cost advantage, and tariffs of 17%-35% have not slowed imports.

earnings_insights: The 42-stock AI basket accounts for 58% of S&P 500 earnings growth since January 2024 (chart reading, Bloomberg, JPMAM, October 7, 2026).
Net interest costs remain at an all-time low share of after-tax corporate profits (NIPA).

macro_indicators.interpretation: Highest of any US state, alongside 3.6% GDP growth over the last year, driven largely by AI.
Third-highest among states, behind New York and Idaho.
First time since 1970 the deficit exceeds 5% of GDP while the economy is expanding.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Up from almost zero through 2022, showing growth dependence on information processing equipment and software.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Rise attributed to sticky inflation, hyperscaler debt issuance and above-expected GDP growth.

risk_factors: Extreme concentration of S&P 500 earnings, returns and capex in 42 AI stocks.
A decline in planned data center projects, since AI is the only growing construction category.
Rising 10-year yields from sticky inflation, hyperscaler debt issuance and strong GDP, with a federal deficit above 5% of GDP during an expansion.
A possible bond market disruption, rating agency downgrade or lower foreign official demand for Treasuries.
Private credit stress, estimated at about 5% (Cliffwater) to about 15% (JPMAM BDC measure), with 70% of amended PIK loans not returning to cash pay.
European deindustrialization and Chinese auto share gains.
EU-China trade escalation involving rare earths and anti-dumping probes.
Cyber risk from open-weight AI models whose safety controls can be removed cheaply.
SpaceX IPO lockup expirations with only about 20% of shares in the free float.
charts_described: Chart shows the 42-stock AI basket accounts for 67% of S&P 500 price return, 58% of earnings growth and 81% of capex/R&D growth since January 2024.
Chart shows the share of S&P 500 companies outperforming the index on a 3-year trailing basis at around 30%, one of the lowest since 1991.
Chart shows the 10-year Treasury yield rising after the August 19 Twist operation announcement.
VW plant table shows manufacturing labor cost per hour of EUR 74 in Emden, EUR 37 in Palmela and EUR 12 in Tianjin.
Refusal rate chart shows GLM-5.3 (abliterated) refusing harmful requests at close to 0%.
Chart shows private credit stress about 5% per Cliffwater and about 15% on the JPMAM BDC measure, with write-offs of 1%-2%.
vol_and_positioning: 60% of S&P 500 stocks are 20% or more below their all-time highs while the index is within 1% of its all-time high, a very wide gap versus history since 1990.
Only 30% of S&P 500 stocks outperform the index on a 3-year trailing basis, one of the lowest readings since 1991.
geopolitical: EU is reportedly prepared to impose Section 301-style tariffs on China unless China meets demands on voluntary export restrictions, rare earth export licenses, overcapacity and market access.
China has begun anti-dumping investigations into European exports and exports more rare earths and permanent magnets to Germany alone than to the US.
Chinese EV imports into Europe continue to grow despite 17%-35% tariffs.
The report header cites an 'Iran War Tracker', but the text provided contains no discussion of it.
cross_bank_references: Goldman Sachs is cited as the source for Chinese auto brand market share changes in Europe (July 2025 to July 2026).
Cliffwater Research is cited for the private credit stress measure of about 5%.

tension_points.bull_case: Tech returns since January 2024 have been driven by earnings growth rather than multiple expansion, which the author says makes markets less susceptible to rapid declines. Corporate net interest costs are at an all-time low share of profits.
tension_points.bear_case: 42 AI stocks account for 60%-80% of S&P earnings growth, returns and capex, 60% of S&P stocks are down 20% or more from highs, and AI is the only growing construction category.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A decline in planned data center projects, which the author says is something to watch.

tension_points.theme: US federal debt and rising yields
tension_points.bull_case: The current rise in yields reflects sticky inflation, hyperscaler debt issuance and above-expected GDP growth, not the 'Final Act'. Budget restructuring is more likely than Fed debt monetization and would be positive long run.
tension_points.bear_case: The deficit is above 5% of GDP during an expansion, and 100% of federal tax revenues are projected to go to entitlements and interest by 2030-2031.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A bond market riot combined with a rating agency downgrade and reduced foreign official demand for Treasuries.
